newsitem.title: POLAND: Gdansk workers protest for shipyard rescue.
newsitem.headline: Gdansk workers protest for shipyard rescue.

text.p: Thousands of workers from the Gdansk shipyard marched through the city Wednesday to demand government aid to save the yard, the birthplace of the union that helped bring down Polish communism.

The protests by workers from the Solidarity trade union, which started on Monday, escalated as marchers chanting slogans took to the streets and at least three workers went on a hunger strike, organisers said.

The union has accused the government of planning to let the state-controlled shipyard sink under its debts to destroy a hotbed of opposition. But the government, dominated by ex-communists, has said it cannot keep subsidising an inefficient company.
The workers want the government to provide guarantees for banks to finance the completion of existing contracts to build five ships while an investor is sought to save the shipyard.
The government said it was standing firm.

"The government will not give guarantees for the Gdansk shipyard as there is no bank willing to grant credits for the enterprise's further operations," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told reporters in Warsaw.
The treasury and industry ministries were due to hold talks on Thursday on a possible future investor.
So far the ministry has not commented on the only offer, from Laman Poland, which represents a Norwegian shipyard, to acquire the Gdansk yard for $20 million over 10 years.
One Polish bank, Bank Gdanski, said it was not interested in financing the entire yard, but might consider offering credits for specific shipbuilding projects.
Three workers went on a hunger strike accepting liquids only, Jerzy Borowczak, the head of the yard's Solidarity branch, told Reuters.

About 2,000 of the 5,000 employees still working at the yard, where Solidarity arose under Lech Walesa's leadership in 1980 to defy communist rule, marched to municipal government offices chanting, "We want work," and other slogans.
About 300 workers have been occupying the offices since Monday in protest. Borowczak said they would stay overnight.
But he said the union would suspend protest marches until Friday, when the next round of talks with the Treasury Ministry, responsible for state assets, were due to be held.

Cimoszewicz, who heads a cabinet dominated by ex-communists, said the government might reconsider if a suitable bank or investor could be found. But he warned that if the union continued to "politicize" the issue it might deter investors.
